title: Oracle Cloud Launches New Nvidia Vera CPUs to Enable OpenAI AI Agent Production
summary:
Oracle has made the general availability of its Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and standalone Vera CPUs on its cloud infrastructure effective Oct. 27. The cloud provider outlined an initial supply of 150,000 Vera CPUs for the current quarter, enabling customers to scale compute and GPU resources independently for the first time. OpenAI is bringing these processors into production to run code and tools within its agentic sandboxes, citing tests that showed 2.2x memory bandwidth per thread and 51% higher Python throughput compared to leading x86 CPUs.

The launch is part of a broader expansion of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) to include a variety of specialized hardware, including a plan to scale Vera Rubin superclusters to multi-gigawatt capacity and the introduction of HGX Rubin NVL8 systems featuring Intel Xeon 6 CPUs. Oracle is also deepening its chip diversification by adding inference systems from Cerebras and SambaNova, and it will become the first hyperscaler outside Google to host custom TPU 8t and 8i chips starting in 2027.

selectedTweets.text:
Oracle $ORCL announced several AI partnerships and infrastructure updates at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas today.

Here's a breakdown of the major announcements:

- $NVDA: Expanding NVIDIA Vera Rubin Superclusters to multi-gigawatt scale. Vera Rubin NVL72 systems and Vera CPUs are now available on Oracle Cloud.

- $GOOGL: Bringing Google's custom TPU chips to Oracle Cloud starting in 2027, making Oracle the first hyperscaler outside Google to offer them. This includes TPU 8t for training and TPU 8i for inference.

- $CBRS: Partnering with Cerebras to bring high-speed AI inference systems to Oracle Cloud in 2027.

- SambaNova: Adding another specialized AI inference chip option to Oracle's cloud infrastructure.

- OpenAI: Expanding their partnership with four enterprise offerings that integrate ChatGPT and Codex into business workflows, cybersecurity, application development, and small-business operations.

- $SNOW: Bringing Snowflake's AI Data Cloud to Oracle Cloud as a native, first-party service, with customers able to purchase and manage it directly through Oracle.

$CBRS and $ORCL are teaming up to bring Cerebras AI inference to Oracle Cloud in 2027.

As Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman says “every step an agent makes requires inference” which means speed matters even more as agents take on longer and more complex tasks.

And that's what makes Oracle saying “AI inference demands choice” so interesting because Cerebras doesn't need to replace $NVDA or $AMD to win a meaningful share of AI workloads where speed matters most.

selectedTweets.text:
- $NVDA and $ORCL announced general availability of Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPUs on OCI on October 27.

- They plan to expand Vera Rubin-based OCI Superclusters to multi-gigawatt scale.

- NVL72 connects 72 GPUs per rack through NVLink.

- The inter-rack network uses Spectrum-6-based Spectrum-X and BlueField-4 DPUs.

- Spectrum-6 provides 102.4Tbps of switching capacity and supports both pluggable optics and CPO configurations.

- OCI also plans to introduce x86-based HGX Rubin NVL8 systems connecting eight Rubin GPUs through NVLink.

- Planned NVL8 specifications include two 64-core Intel Xeon 6 CPUs, 4TB of DDR5 and 6.4Tbps of RDMA networking.

- Oracle outlined an initial supply of 150,000 Vera CPUs and availability in select regions this quarter.

- OCI Kubernetes Engine supports independent scaling of CPU and GPU resources.

- OpenAI says it is bringing Vera CPUs on OCI into production for code and tool execution in agentic sandboxes.

> $NVDA is expanding its share of each customer's AI infrastructure spending by supplying standalone CPUs and networking alongside GPUs.

> When an agent's CPU tasks block its next model call, adding CPU capacity could reduce cost per task more effectively than buying additional GPUs.

> Shorter tool-execution waits could also reduce how long KV caches occupy GPU memory, linking CPU performance to inference memory efficiency.

> Independent CPU and GPU scaling lets customers adjust resource ratios by workload, with benefits to be validated through actual GPU utilization and agent completion times.

> NVL8 offers x86 compatibility and a smaller deployment unit, but communication beyond eight GPUs depends more heavily on RDMA network performance outside its local NVLink domain.

> The planned Xeon 6 deployment shows that $INTC retains host CPU supply opportunities as Vera adoption expands.

> The optical supply chain depends on port speeds, network tier counts and optical connectivity choices alongside GPU volumes; Spectrum-6 adoption alone does not confirm OCI's use of CPO or orders for any particular optical supplier.

> $ORCL's investment returns depend on how quickly announced gigawatts become operating, billable capacity; this announcement disclosed no total expansion capacity, CAPEX or completion timeline.
